title: Distinguishable Deletion: Unifying Knowledge Erasure and Refusal for Large Language Model Unlearning
claim: Existing approaches either delete knowledge unstably or refuse while leaving knowledge intact; ours deletes at the distribution level and refuses reliably.
layout: 4 quadrant panels, color-coded borders, blue/red prior versus green ours, histograms at bottom
description: The figure is a 2x2 grid of dashed-border panels. The top-left blue panel shows Distinguishable Refusal (DR). A frozen LLM with a snowflake icon maps retain and unlearn sample clusters through a prompt template. An attacker icon then triggers a leaked answer, so the forgotten knowledge persists. The bottom-left red panel shows Knowledge Deletion (KD). A fire-marked LLM, shifted energy distributions, and a list of bad outputs appear: hallucination, gibberish, and an incoherent answer. A single green preferred answer is also listed. The top-right green panel shows the proposed D2/EUA pipeline. Blue and orange sample dots pass through the model and a prompt, and energy-index curves separate the two groups. Attacks still produce refusals. The bottom-right panel has three bar-chart histograms of vocabulary probabilities. They compare KD after unlearning, before unlearning, and D2 after unlearning. Red, blue, and green color-code the three paradigms.
caption: Motivation and overview of our work. Left: Existing unlearning methods fall short in overall performance and general reliability: KD-based unlearning often produces unstable outputs, while DR-based unlearning is highly vulnerable to adversarial attacks. Right: These limitations in practicality and reliability motivate us to explore a new unlearning paradigm, Distinguishable Deletion (D2), equipped with an Energy-based Unlearning Alignment (EUA) method. Rather than focusing on specific token sequence suppression, D2 achieves a distribution-level unlearning paradigm that characterizes knowledge presence via an energy-based index, enabling reliable deletion and refusal of unlearned content while maintaining superior performance on retained knowledge.
abstract: Mitigating sensitive and harmful outputs is fundamental to ensuring safe deployment of LLMs. Existing approaches typically follow two paradigms: Knowledge Deletion (KD), which erases undesirable information during training, and Distinguishable Refusal (DR), which steers models away from using sensitive knowledge during inference. Despite rapid progress, KD-based unlearning struggles with biased deletion due to suppressing specific token sequences as a substitute for complete knowledge removal, whereas DR-based unlearning risks the re-emergence of harmful knowledge because the underlying knowledge remains intact. To address these issues, we propose Distinguishable Deletion ($\mathrm{D^2}$), a paradigm that restricts the response distribution in the latent representation rather than specific tokens to erase undesirable knowledge, while distinguishing it from retained knowledge, enabling a refusal mechanism to handle unlearned inputs safely and coherently. To implement $\mathrm{D^2}$, we introduce an energy index that quantifies the presence of knowledge and the separation between unlearned and retained content. Mathematical and empirical analyses show that energy is both accurate and efficient, enabling Energy-based Unlearning Alignment (EUA) to enforce energy-boundary unlearning during training and apply an energy-based refusal mechanism at inference. Extensive experiments demonstrate that EUA significantly outperforms previous methods, indicating the superiority of $\mathrm{D^2}$. Our code is available at https://github.com/Puning97/EUA-for-LLM-Unlearning.
